Chapter 8: Bearing Witness — The Journalist’s Dilemma.
You know, to watch and to write means carrying a real burden. Journalists move through Africa not just as observers, but as participants—even if they’re always aware of how much they might be missing. The stories they bring back are never the whole truth. They’re really just fragments—moments caught in passing.
Picture this: a reporter sitting on a crowded bus, notebook in hand. The road’s bumpy, the trip seems endless. All around, people share stories—about lost jobs, faraway family, and their hopes for what’s next. The reporter listens and scribbles, but deep down, he knows he’ll never capture it all. The real story? It’s always so much bigger than what ends up on the page.
Then there’s a photographer in a refugee camp, trying to document everyday life. He’s careful, respectful—but he can’t shake the feeling he’s intruding. The people in his photos, they’re more than just their struggles. They’re more than the images that might show up in distant newspapers. He’s left wondering: what does it really mean to bear witness, to tell someone else’s story?
Sometimes, a government official sits down for an interview—eager to shape the story before it’s even written. The official’s words are polished, cautious, steering clear of anything too controversial. But the journalist can sense the gaps—the things left unsaid. He tries to read between the lines, searching for the truth hidden beneath the surface.
Later at night, the journalist thinks back on the day. He recalls the faces, the voices, those moments of real connection—and sometimes, misunderstanding. He knows his very presence changes things. Even his questions shape the answers he gets. That line between just watching and actually participating? It’s never quite clear.
Most people don’t realize just how much power there is in telling a story. Choosing what to include and what to leave out—well, that shapes reality itself. And that’s the heart of the journalist’s dilemma: to do justice to the people he meets, to honor their full complexity, and to resist the urge to make things too simple.
So here’s the key takeaway: bearing witness isn’t just a privilege. It’s a real responsibility. The stories of Africa—they aren’t his to own, but to share. And that means sharing them with care, with humility, and with a deep respect for everyone involved.
